title: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code
summary: The AI made the source generator put `[ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on every formatter and resolver it emits, inside `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. It edited the 6 code templates and one helper (TransformUtilities.cs), re-recorded 222 test snapshots, and added a test file and a README note.
head: a0aa5ab2

claims.claim: Of the 222 changed snapshot files, 220 change only by added attribute and #if/#endif guard lines; the other 2 are both in Resources/GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember/ (Named: the brace moves to its own line; Ordinal: one extra blank line).
claims.why_this_tier: The evidence is a count from the diff classifier script; it describes the diff and does not by itself show the snapshots are right.

claims.claim: All 222 changed snapshots are exactly what the branch's generator emits, and the emitted code compiles: the snapshot test project passes 169 of 169 on the branch (base: 167 of 167).
claims.why_this_tier: Regeneration on the real artefact: the snapshot tests run the generator and compare its output text with the committed files, then compile it, and they pass.

claims.claim: The 6 committed template .cs files emit the same text as their edited .tt files: dotnet-t4 regeneration matches 6 of 6 on the branch, the same method matches 6 of 6 untouched templates on base, and the negative control differs 6 of 6.
claims.why_this_tier: A deterministic regeneration of the real templates, compared on the emitted text after layout normalisation and calibrated on base; it is not a byte-for-byte match with Visual Studio's tool.

claims.claim: For a sample with an int-keyed object, a string-keyed object, an enum, a union and a resolver, every generated file contains the attribute and every occurrence sits inside the guard.
claims.why_this_tier: The 2 new CodeCoverageExclusionTests fail on base (2 of 2) and pass on the branch.

claims.claim: The TransformUtilities.cs edit is required: without it, a formatter nested in a generic type with constraints is emitted as `{#if ...` on one line and the generated code fails to compile (CS1040).
claims.why_this_tier: Reverting only that line makes GenerationTests.GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember fail (168 of 169 pass) and restoring it makes it pass; a hand run shows the failure is a CS1040 compile error.

chain.link: edit reverted: the snapshot test fails (script)
the failure is CS1040 in generated code (hand run)

claims.claim: The TransformUtilities.cs edit has one visible side effect in the snapshots: one extra blank line in the Ordinal formatter of GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember.
claims.why_this_tier: Counted by the classifier and confirmed by the removal run; that the blank line is harmless (and that EnumTemplate gets the same blank line, by reading) is not machine-checked.

claims.claim: The generator now puts [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on the user-declared partial resolver classes (ResolverTemplate, CompositeResolverTemplate), whose accessibility the user picks and which can be public; a user who already excluded their partial resolver by hand gets compile error CS0579 on the branch.
claims.why_this_tier: It touches public API, so no machine may settle it: the attribute lands in the consumer's public type metadata and breaks the build for an existing, plausible user pattern (shown on the real generator: probe passes on base, fails on branch), which is a public API and compatibility call, not a machine call.
claims.owner_role: MessagePack-CSharp maintainer who owns public API and breaking changes

claims.claim: Agent's claim: the guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` is needed because the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework.
claims.why_this_tier: Only the agent's word backs it, and our check contradicts it: the attribute is in the netstandard2.0 and net472 reference assemblies and an unguarded probe compiles on both, so the guard drops the feature on 2 targets; widening it is a product call.

claims.claim: README: all generated formatters and resolvers carry [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage], emitted only where available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework).
claims.why_this_tier: Documentation is not machine-checked; its first sentence matches C-2297-04, its second repeats the availability statement that attribute-availability.json contradicts.

claims.claim: The snapshot check is line-ending sensitive and passes here because .gitattributes checks the 225 snapshot .cs files out with CRLF; with LF snapshots 89 of 169 tests fail.
claims.why_this_tier: A count from running the tests on a scratch copy with snapshots converted to LF; it qualifies C-2297-02 rather than backing a change.

found: The diff classifier (script) flagged 2 of 222 snapshots that change beyond attribute and guard lines, both in Resources/GenericDataTypeWithPrivateMember/: Named (the line `{\tinternal sealed class ...` is split so `{` stands alone) and Ordinal (one added blank line).

The TransformUtilities.cs edit has no stated reason (the commit message has no body). We found it is required: with it reverted, the generated code fails with CS1040; its one visible side effect is the extra blank line in the Ordinal snapshot.

We found the guard too strict: ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in the netstandard2.0 and net472 reference assemblies, so netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers silently get no exclusion. The README and the test comment state the opposite.

We found a break for existing users: a hand-written [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on the user's partial resolver compiles on base and fails with CS0579 (duplicate attribute) on the branch. No branch test covers it.
CodeCoverageExclusionTests hard-codes the guard text, so widening the guard also means changing the test.
By reading the test verifier: no preprocessor symbols are set in the snapshot compilations, so the guarded-out path (netstandard2.0, .NET Framework) is never compiled by the tests.

The diff classifier (script) flagged 1 Resources directory with no test method (Resources/InterfaceUnion/, 3 files). It already exists on base, is not run by any test, and the branch leaves it without the attribute, so it is now stale.
Correction to the handoff: the verifier writes actual output to Resources/ only when WRITE_EXPECTED is defined (the method is [Conditional("WRITE_EXPECTED")]); a plain test run only compares.
When generated content differs, the test framework reports 'Expected source file list to match' rather than the content diff, which hides the real cause (here CS1040).

refused.what: [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] added to the user-declared partial resolver classes (C-2297-07)
refused.why: It changes the consumer's public type metadata and breaks the build (CS0579) for users who already excluded their resolver by hand. That is a public API and compatibility call, so the owner decides.

scope_drift: None found. The TransformUtilities.cs edit looked like drift (it has no stated reason) but the removal test shows the feature does not compile without it.
not_checked: The text of issue #2297: we could not read it here, so R-2297-1..4 are inferred from the branch title and commit.
macOS: all runs were on Linux (6.18.44, x86_64). Per .gitattributes the snapshots check out as CRLF on every OS, but that was not run on a Mac.
Compiling real generated output for netstandard2.0, netstandard2.1 or net472 consumers: only a small probe was compiled for those targets.
Whether coverage tools (coverlet, dotnet-coverage) actually drop the generated types from their reports.
Unity, Mono and other builds with their own preprocessor symbols; netstandard1.x and .NET Framework before 4.0.
Union and enum formatters nested in a generic type with constraints: no snapshot covers them; the need for the edit (Union) and the blank line (Enum) are by reading only.
Byte-for-byte equality with Visual Studio's TextTemplatingFilePreprocessor: dotnet-t4 was compared on emitted text only.
